title: Emotional literacy in special schools
official: Effectiveness of a special school mental health intervention for children with learning disabilities
summary:
Background and study aims
Children with learning disabilities are more likely than other children to have mental health problems. Many children with learning disabilities go to special schools. There are currently no mental health programmes with good research evidence for children with learning disabilities in special schools. This means that children with learning disabilities are often left out of plans to promote good mental health at school. 
We will test whether a mental health programme for children with learning disabilities in special schools helps to improve their mental health. The programme focuses on learning about emotions. The programme is called Zippy’s Friends for Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (ZF-SEND). We will also test if Zippy’s Friends-SEND (ZF-SEND) leads to improvements in mental health that make it worthwhile to spend time and money using the programme. This is usually called ‘cost-effectiveness’. 

Who can participate?
Children 8-12 years of age who are in/will be in the class(es) identified by eligible schools taking part in the study, their parents and carers and school staff

What does the study involve?
We will find 66 special schools from across the UK. We will assign schools by chance (like flipping a coin) to deliver ZF-SEND for a whole school year or to carry on with what they currently do to support mental health. Each school will be asked to select about 10 children with learning disabilities aged 8-12 years to take part in the study. We will also invite their parents and carers and school staff to participate.
 We will collect information about the children’s mental health from teachers, the children themselves, and their parents before the programme starts and at the end of the school year. We will also collect information about other things that might change – like children’s understanding of emotions. At the end, we will look to see if mental health is better in the children who are taught with ZF-SEND. We will also talk to children, teachers and parents to ask about how ZF-SEND worked for them (or not). We will find out how much time and other resources are needed to deliver ZF-SEND in special schools. We can then work out how much it costs to deliver. 

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
By taking part in this study, participants will be helping to answer whether Zippy’s Friends might be beneficial for children with learning disability in special schools. The results of this study may benefit children and their families in the future.
Taking part does require some time. This study will not pose any risk to parents/carers or children. However, some people find it helpful to think or talk about their experiences, but some may find this upsetting.

Where is the study run from?
The study is being organised and led by researchers at the University of Birmingham, King's College London, Queen's University Belfast, the University of the West of Scotland, the University of South Wales, and Cardiff University (UK).

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
March 2027 to July 2028

Who is funding the study?
This study is funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) Public Health Research Programme (project reference NIHR508686). The views expressed are those of the author(s) and not necessarily those of the NIHR or the Department of Health and Social Care (UK).

Who is the main contact?
Dr Linda Adara, ELISS@cardiff.ac.uk

interventions.name:
Zippy’s Friends for Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (ZF-SEND) is a manualised, curriculum-based programme that aims to develop children’s repertoire of coping skills and their ability to adapt those coping skills to various situations. 
The ZF-SEND manual consists of six modules: Feelings

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
SEND schools:  
1. Special schools will be eligible if they have at least one class primarily for children with moderate to severe learning disabilities in the relevant age range (8-12 years)
2. Schools will require headteacher (or other senior level depending on the relevant governance arrangements) agreement to take part in the trial
3. Schools must be providing school day educational provision as a state-funded school or an independent special school approved under relevant legislation (e.g., Section 41 of the Children and Families Act 2014 in England and Wales), and be located geographically in England, Wales, Scotland, or Northern Ireland

Child participants:  
1. Children 8-12 years of age who are in/will be in the class(es) identified by eligible schools taking part in the trial
2. Children taking part in the research (through teacher, parent/carer, and child completed outcomes) must have relevant informed consent in place and, in the case of child-reported outcomes, assent from the child

Teaching staff:
1. Teachers and teaching assistants must be working at least one day in a typical school week in the class(es) identified by eligible schools taking part in the trial
2. Teachers/other teaching staff must provide informed consent for their participation (to complete the measures, for those in the ZF-SEND arm to provide data about their delivery of the intervention and for a selected sample, to participate in an interview)

Parent/carer participants:  
1. Parents/guardians/carers will be the biological parents or legal guardians of eligible children
2. Will have a level of English language enabling (verbal) completion of outcome measures or to complete key measures in other languages where formal translations are available
3. Parent/guardians/carers must provide informed consent for their participation
Exclusion criteria:
SEND schools:  
1. Schools delivering any manualised or curriculum-based emotional literacy or mental health programme over at least a full school term

Child participants:  
1. No parental/carer consent to participate in the research (although this would not exclude the child from the intervention)
2. If the child is unable to assent or to communicate using English (and adaptations to meet their communication needs cannot be put in place in the classroom setting) they will be excluded from completion of child-reported outcomes

Teaching staff participants: 
1. No informed consent received

Parent/carer participants:  
1. Current child protection concerns relating to the child at the point of recruitment or the family are reported by the school to be in a state of current crisis
2. Insufficient command of the (spoken) English language to complete the outcome measures or no official translated versions of key measures available in required language
3. Lacking capacity to give informed consent
4. No informed consent received
